shortDescription: In Pontus, Gregory, a pupil of Origen, was a bishop and wrote rules for his churches after a raid by the Goths. In Lycia, Methodius, bishop of Olympus, wrote the Banquet, where ten virgins praise chastity.

timeline.when: While Origen taught at Caesarea in Palestine
timeline.headline: Gregory and his brother study with Origen, and Gregory thanks him in a farewell speech

lines.text: Gregory writes that he set out with his brother to take their sister to her husband, and that the journey let them go on to Berytus to study law.
lines.reference: Gregory, Address to Origen 5, cic/texts/anf06_gregory-thaumaturgus-dionysius-julius-africanus-methodius-arnobius.xml lines 2855-2869

lines.text: Eusebius writes that while Origen taught at Caesarea, pupils came to him from other countries, among them Theodorus, later called Gregory, and his brother Athenodorus. Origen turned them from Greek and Roman learning to philosophy and the study of God. After five years with him, both were made bishops in Pontus while still young.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VI.30, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 36568-36584

lines.text: Jerome writes that after five years with Origen, the brothers were sent home to their mother, and that Theodorus, on leaving, gave a speech of thanks to Origen before a large gathering, with Origen there.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 65, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40775-40787; written in 392, lines 38784-38785, a conversion from the fourteenth year of Theodosius, counting his reign from 379
lines.note: Jerome says the speech still exists in his day.

timeline.when: As bishop in Pontus, in the time of Gallienus
timeline.headline: Gregory leads the churches of Pontus, and joins the bishops against Paul at Antioch

lines.text: Eusebius writes that Gregory and his brother Athenodorus, friends of Origen, were then leading the churches of Pontus.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VII.14, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 40580-40588; Gallienus, VII.13, lines 40566-40569

lines.text: Eusebius writes that bishops came from all sides to Antioch against Paul of Samosata, bishop there, who held that Christ was by nature a common man. Among the most eminent, he names Gregory and Athenodorus, pastors of the churches of Pontus.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VII.27-28, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 41835-41874

lines.text: Jerome writes that Gregory wrote a short paraphrase of Ecclesiastes, and that report told of letters by him and of the signs and wonders he worked as bishop.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 65, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40789-40793
lines.note: The wonders are Jerome's report of what was said.

lines.text: Gregory of Nyssa writes that when Gregory was given the city, no more than seventeen of its many people and those around it had received the faith.
lines.reference: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Gregory the Wonderworker, cic/texts/gregory-nyssa_opera-omnia-pg46-grc-lat_migne1863.txt lines 66362-66366
lines.note: Written late in the 4th century. The Greek print is damaged.

timeline.when: After a raid by the Boradi and Goths, date unknown
timeline.headline: Gregory writes rules for a church after the raid
timeline.witness: Gregory, Canonical Letter, his own words

lines.text: Gregory writes to a bishop he calls most holy father that captives who ate what their captors set before them bear no blame, since all report that the raiders did not sacrifice to idols.
lines.reference: Gregory, Canonical Letter, canon 1, cic/texts/anf06_gregory-thaumaturgus-dionysius-julius-africanus-methodius-arnobius.xml lines 2005-2013

lines.text: Gregory writes that women forced by the raiders are without sin if their past life was chaste, as with the young woman in Deuteronomy who cried out and had no one to help her.
lines.reference: Gregory, Canonical Letter, canon 1, cic/texts/anf06_gregory-thaumaturgus-dionysius-julius-africanus-methodius-arnobius.xml lines 2018-2034

lines.text: Gregory writes that those who used the raid, a time of ruin for all, to enrich themselves are to be cut off from the church.
lines.reference: Gregory, Canonical Letter, canon 2, cic/texts/anf06_gregory-thaumaturgus-dionysius-julius-africanus-methodius-arnobius.xml lines 2046-2056

lines.text: Gregory writes that keeping others' property as payment for what one has lost makes a man a Boradus or a Goth to others.
lines.reference: Gregory, Canonical Letter, canon 5, cic/texts/anf06_gregory-thaumaturgus-dionysius-julius-africanus-methodius-arnobius.xml lines 2132-2136

lines.text: Gregory writes that some are said to have held by force captives who had escaped, and he tells the bishop to send men into the country to deal with it.
lines.reference: Gregory, Canonical Letter, canon 6, cic/texts/anf06_gregory-thaumaturgus-dionysius-julius-africanus-methodius-arnobius.xml lines 2151-2158

lines.text: Gregory writes of those who joined the raiders, forgetting they were men of Pontus and Christians, and killed their own people and showed the raiders roads and houses. They are barred even from hearing the Scriptures in church until a council of bishops decides.
lines.reference: Gregory, Canonical Letter, canon 7, cic/texts/anf06_gregory-thaumaturgus-dionysius-julius-africanus-methodius-arnobius.xml lines 2166-2178

lines.text: Gregory writes that those who broke into others' houses, and then came forward and gave the goods back, are to be placed among the penitents. Those who kept what the raiders left behind, and did the same, may join in prayer.
lines.reference: Gregory, Canonical Letter, canons 8-9, cic/texts/anf06_gregory-thaumaturgus-dionysius-julius-africanus-methodius-arnobius.xml lines 2185-2204

lines.text: Gregory's Canonical Letter, as it has come down, ends with an eleventh canon. It sets out four stages for a penitent: weeping outside the church door, hearing the Scriptures in the porch, then standing inside and leaving with those still being taught the faith, and at last joining the faithful and sharing the sacrament.
lines.reference: Gregory, Canonical Letter, canon 11, cic/texts/anf06_gregory-thaumaturgus-dionysius-julius-africanus-methodius-arnobius.xml lines 2227-2246

timeline.headline: Methodius, bishop of Olympus, writes the Banquet and argues against Origen

lines.text: Jerome writes that Methodius, bishop of Olympus in Lycia and later of Tyre, wrote Against Porphyry, a Banquet of the ten virgins, On the Resurrection against Origen, and On Free Will, also against Origen.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 83, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 41095-41102

lines.text: In Methodius's Banquet, Gregorion tells Euboulios of a banquet where ten virgins, Marcella, Theophila, Thaleia, Theopatra, Thallousa, Agathe, Procilla, Thekla, Tusiane and Domnina, each spoke on chastity. Arete, Virtue, the daughter of Philosophy, is with them.
lines.reference: Methodius, Banquet of the Ten Virgins, introduction, cic/texts/anf06_gregory-thaumaturgus-dionysius-julius-africanus-methodius-arnobius.xml lines 29838-29900

lines.text: In Methodius's Banquet, Arete bids the virgins rise and sing a hymn of thanks. Thekla leads, and the others answer with the refrain: I keep myself pure for you, O Bridegroom, and holding a lighted torch I go to meet you.
lines.reference: Methodius, Banquet of the Ten Virgins XI.2, cic/texts/anf06_gregory-thaumaturgus-dionysius-julius-africanus-methodius-arnobius.xml lines 34172-34180

lines.text: Socrates writes that Methodius, bishop of Olympus in Lycia, railed against Origen in various places, and afterwards, as if taking it all back, praised him in a dialogue named Xenon.
lines.reference: Socrates, Church History VI.13, cic/texts/npnf202_socrates-sozomen-ecclesiastical-histories.xml lines 18141-18154
lines.note: Socrates wrote in the 5th century, and defends Origen.

lines.when: at the end of the last persecution, or under Decius and Valerian
lines.text: Jerome writes that Methodius was crowned with martyrdom at Chalcis in Greece, at the end of the recent persecution or, as others say, in the reign of Decius and Valerian.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 83, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 41102-41105

timeline.headline: Basil of Caesarea names Gregory's words and customs as his church's own

lines.text: Basil writes to the people of Neocaesarea that his grandmother Macrina, who came from them, taught him as a child the words of Gregory, as far as memory had kept them.
lines.reference: Basil, Letter 204, to the Neocaesareans, cic/texts/npnf208_basil-letters-select-works.xml lines 37060-37065

lines.text: Basil writes that only seventeen Christians were handed over to Gregory, and that he brought the whole people of town and country to God. He tells that Gregory, in Christ's name, turned rivers from their course and dried up a lake.
lines.reference: Basil, On the Holy Spirit 74, cic/texts/npnf208_basil-letters-select-works.xml lines 14657-14666

lines.text: Basil writes that the churches Gregory led added nothing to what he left them. The form of the doxology, the church's words of praise to God, which some now object to, is one of his customs, Basil says, kept on his authority.
lines.reference: Basil, On the Holy Spirit 74, cic/texts/npnf208_basil-letters-select-works.xml lines 14680-14691

lines.text: Answering the clergy of Neocaesarea, who said his practices were unknown in Gregory's time, Basil writes that their own litanies were unknown then too, and that they have kept none of his customs.
lines.reference: Basil, Letter 207, to the clergy of Neocaesarea, cic/texts/npnf208_basil-letters-select-works.xml lines 37308-37323

uncertain: Who made Gregory a bishop, and when. Eusebius says both brothers were made bishops in Pontus after five years with Origen. Jerome says Origen sent them home to their mother. Neither gives a year.
The raid's year. The Canonical Letter names the Boradi and Goths, and gives no year. The old sources held here do not date it.
The eleventh canon. It differs from the ten before it: it answers no case from the raid, and sets out the four stages of a penitent. The old sources held here do not say who wrote it.
The seventeen. Basil says seventeen Christians were handed over to Gregory, and Gregory of Nyssa that no more than seventeen had received the faith. Both wrote in the 4th century.
Gregory's wonders. Jerome reports what was said of his signs and wonders. Basil tells of rivers turned and a lake dried. Both wrote in the 4th century.
Methodius's death. Jerome says he was martyred at Chalcis in Greece, at the end of the recent persecution or, as others say, under Decius and Valerian.
Methodius and Origen. Jerome names two books of his against Origen. Socrates, who defends Origen, says Methodius later praised him in a dialogue named Xenon.
